title: Read and write paths
summary: Draw one successful read and one successful write end to end.

parts.rule: After defining the API and data model, walk one important write and one important read from client to response. For each hop, say what key is used, whether the hop is synchronous, where durable success occurs, and what is returned. Add caches, queues, and replicas only at the point where the path explains their job.

Walking a request reveals duplicate writers, missing indexes, cache consistency gaps, and slow dependencies on the user path. It also gives every performance claim a location: latency is the sum of actual synchronous hops, not a property of the picture as a whole.
parts.example: For a URL shortener, the write begins with POST /v1/links {url}. The load balancer sends it to Link Service, which authenticates the owner, validates the URL, generates code a1b2c3d, and inserts links(code=a1b2c3d, owner_id=42, destination_url=...) on the primary database. The service returns 201 only after that insert commits, because acknowledging before durability could hand the user a code that vanishes. Analytics can receive an event later; it is not required for create success. The read begins with GET /a1b2c3d. Redirect Service looks up cache key link:a1b2c3d. On a hit, it returns 302 immediately. On a miss, it performs a primary-key lookup on links.code, verifies disabled_at is null, fills the cache with a 24-hour TTL, and returns 302. Name both branches: a cache hit may take 5 ms while a database miss takes 30 ms, but both produce the same redirect contract. A delete writes disabled_at on the primary and evicts that exact cache key; otherwise the read path can serve a disabled URL. Once the baseline is clear, add a read replica only if read volume requires it and state the resulting lag. This single walk explains the primary key, cache key, acknowledgement boundary, and asynchronous analytics without adding unrelated services.

body:
Rule. After defining the API and data model, walk one important write and one important read from client to response. For each hop, say what key is used, whether the hop is synchronous, where durable success occurs, and what is returned. Add caches, queues, and replicas only at the point where the path explains their job.

Why it matters. A box diagram can look complete while hiding the essential behavior. Walking a request reveals duplicate writers, missing indexes, cache consistency gaps, and slow dependencies on the user path. It also gives every performance claim a location: latency is the sum of actual synchronous hops, not a property of the picture as a whole.

Worked example. For a URL shortener, the write begins with POST /v1/links {url}. The load balancer sends it to Link Service, which authenticates the owner, validates the URL, generates code a1b2c3d, and inserts links(code=a1b2c3d, owner_id=42, destination_url=...) on the primary database. The service returns 201 only after that insert commits, because acknowledging before durability could hand the user a code that vanishes. Analytics can receive an event later; it is not required for create success. The read begins with GET /a1b2c3d. Redirect Service looks up cache key link:a1b2c3d. On a hit, it returns 302 immediately. On a miss, it performs a primary-key lookup on links.code, verifies disabled_at is null, fills the cache with a 24-hour TTL, and returns 302. Name both branches: a cache hit may take 5 ms while a database miss takes 30 ms, but both produce the same redirect contract. A delete writes disabled_at on the primary and evicts that exact cache key; otherwise the read path can serve a disabled URL. Once the baseline is clear, add a read replica only if read volume requires it and state the resulting lag. This single walk explains the primary key, cache key, acknowledgement boundary, and asynchronous analytics without adding unrelated services.

[[diagram:paths]]

When to use. Walk paths immediately after the first data model. Use them to justify indexes, place cache-aside logic, decide which work can move to a queue, and divide an end-to-end latency budget. Re-walk the same request whenever the design gains another dependency or consistency promise.

When to refuse. Do not draw many services without tracing a request through them. Avoid a cache before you can describe the uncached read, and do not merge read and write into one bidirectional arrow. Name the row, partition, or object key being accessed. A path is incomplete if it never says when the user-visible operation has actually succeeded.
